# ViewOwl

> A production content-delivery platform that puts live web pages on fleets of low-cost
> microcontroller displays. A server renders ordinary HTML in a real browser, converts each
> frame to the display's native pixel format, and ships it to ESP32 devices over a custom
> reliability protocol built on UDP. The devices hold no application logic — they receive
> frames and render them — so all content, data, and layout live in HTML/JS on the server.
> Devices are flashed and Wi-Fi-provisioned entirely from the browser; no toolchain, no IDE.

## What makes this non-trivial

ViewOwl owns the full path from a cloud-rendered web page down to silicon — not just a
front-end and back-end, but an additional embedded tier with its own wire protocol and
offline playback engine. The hard problems it solves end-to-end:

- **Reliable frame delivery over lossy Wi-Fi/UDP.** Custom 15-byte-header protocol with
  per-chunk stop-and-wait ACK, sequencing, retransmission, session lifecycle, device-side
  socket resurrection, and watchdog-safe receive loops. UDP here is deliberate, not naïve:
  the payload is bulk binary frames (150–300 KB) to devices with ~300 KB RAM, where MQTT
  (built for small pub/sub telemetry, plus a broker hop and fragile multi-day ESP32 clients)
  and WebSocket/TCP (connection state, socket buffers, head-of-line blocking) both cost RAM
  and reliability the device can't spare — and neither offers frame dedup or atomic offline
  animation without rebuilding exactly this on top. Stop-and-wait means the device never
  buffers more than one packet.
- **CRC32 frame dedup.** The device reports its last-rendered frame's CRC in every HELLO;
  the server answers `NOT_MODIFIED` when nothing changed — no needless re-transmit, no
  flash wear, no visible refresh.
- **Atomic multi-frame animation (Class C).** The server pre-renders an N-frame batch,
  the device writes it to a flash partition and plays the loop **independently of the
  network** — survives Wi-Fi loss entirely.
- **Per-device multi-resolution rendering.** Each template is rendered at every connected
  device's native resolution (320×240 ILI9341, 480×320 ST7796, 480×320 ILI9486).
- **Zero-toolchain onboarding.** Browser-based flashing (Web Serial) and serial
  Wi-Fi/token provisioning persisted to NVS — a non-developer can bring a device online.
- **Self-describing templates + live data.** `data-vow-*` HTML attributes drive the whole
  pipeline; any API-backed page becomes a wall display with no embedded code.
- **Multi-tenant platform, not a single-screen script.** User accounts and roles, guest
  devices, per-user templates, JWT/BCrypt auth, a separate security DB with IP auto-blocking
  (brute-force/scanner thresholds), rate limiting, session fingerprinting, and a real-time
  SignalR dashboard for managing fleets. The server is intentionally heavier than one screen
  needs because it is built to host many users' devices, not one.

## Status

Production-deployed on a Linux ARM64 server behind a TLS reverse proxy. Devices run
continuously for weeks without watchdog reboots; a server redeploy costs at most one
delayed HELLO cycle (NVS-persisted CRC → `NOT_MODIFIED` on reconnect). Actively developed,
with three shipping firmware variants and a documented wire protocol kept byte-compatible
between the C# server and the C firmware (`UDPUtils.cs` ↔ `packet.h`). The live instance
runs on deliberately modest hardware as a standing load test, to surface limits early
rather than hide them.

ViewOwl is the latest project in the **OWLOS** open-source IoT line
([github.com/KirinDenis/owlos](https://github.com/KirinDenis/owlos) — 47 stars, ESP32/ESP8266
firmware & tools), developed with its maker community — an evolution, not a from-scratch
experiment.

## Design rationale (non-obvious choices, learned in production)

Each of these is a response to a real failure mode, not a preference — useful context before
judging the architecture:

- **Custom stop-and-wait reliable-delivery over UDP, not MQTT/TCP.** A minimal discrete-frame
  transport, deliberately NOT windowed and NOT a byte stream — closer to "reliable file copy,
  one packet at a time" than a TCP reimplementation. Stop-and-wait is the point: the device
  never holds a reassembly window, so RAM stays bounded. MQTT (broker hop, small-message
  model, fragile multi-day ESP32 clients) and TCP/WebSocket (head-of-line blocking, socket
  buffers) are the wrong fit for pushing 150–300 KB frames to a ~300 KB-RAM device, and
  neither gives frame dedup or atomic offline animation for free.
- **CRC dedup is essential, and the variant must match byte-for-byte.** Re-sending unchanged
  frames wears flash, stalls the player, and flickers. A single mismatched CRC32 variant
  between server and firmware silently disables `NOT_MODIFIED` and forces a full re-download
  every cycle (a real, fixed bug: `esp_rom_crc32_le` is standard zlib CRC32, not
  init=0/no-finalXOR).
- **Animation is pre-rendered to flash, not streamed.** Live streaming dies on any Wi-Fi
  hiccup; flash playback makes motion network-independent.
- **Per-device-resolution rendering.** A frame at the wrong resolution crops, not scales.
- **Class-C templates must be deterministic** (no `Math.random()`/clock) or the dedup CRC
  never matches and the device re-downloads forever.

In practice the UDP transport is the stable layer (runs for months); the hard, evolving
engineering is the rendering/grab side (headless-browser memory, grab scheduling, frame
determinism).

## Architecture

Three components communicating through the filesystem and UDP:

1. **Grabber** (`ViewOwl.Grabber.WebAPI/`) — ASP.NET Core 8 service. Runs headless Chromium, renders HTML → PNG → BGR565 `.bin`. Serves templates over HTTP (Chromium ARM64 blocks `file://`). Port 5000/TCP.
2. **UDP Server** (`ViewOwl.UDP.Server/`) — .NET 8 console. Listens for ESP32 HELLO packets, streams `.bin` files via a custom 15-byte header ACK protocol. Port 11000/UDP.
3. **Firmware** (`ViewOwl.ESP32.Client/`) — ESP-IDF 5.5 C99. WiFi + UDP client + SPI LCD driver + flash playback engine. Three build variants: 320×240 (ILI9341), 480×320 (ST7796), 480×320 (ILI9486).

Shared state: `ExchangeFolder/` — Grabber writes `{guid}.bin`, UDP Server reads it. Both on same machine. Atomic writes (`.tmp` → rename).

## Key source files

- [`ViewOwl.Grabber.Engine/Chrome.cs`](ViewOwl.Grabber.Engine/Chrome.cs) — PNG capture, BGR565 conversion, CRC dedup
- [`ViewOwl.Grabber.WebAPI/BackgroundServices/DeviceTemplateRefreshWorker.cs`](ViewOwl.Grabber.WebAPI/BackgroundServices/DeviceTemplateRefreshWorker.cs) — periodic re-grab, Class C multi-frame batch, HTML hash skip
- [`ViewOwl.UDP.Server/UDPServer.cs`](ViewOwl.UDP.Server/UDPServer.cs) — session lifecycle, NOT_MODIFIED CRC optimisation
- [`ViewOwl.UDP.Server/UDPServerSession.cs`](ViewOwl.UDP.Server/UDPServerSession.cs) — per-device frame transfer, CRC32 computation
- [`ViewOwl.UDP.Utils/UDPUtils.cs`](ViewOwl.UDP.Utils/UDPUtils.cs) — 15-byte PacketHeader (must stay in sync with `packet.h`)
- [`ViewOwl.ESP32.Client/main/udp_client.c`](ViewOwl.ESP32.Client/main/udp_client.c) — HELLO/AUTH/DATA/ACK/DONE, batch flash write, NVS CRC persistence
- [`ViewOwl.ESP32.Client/main/config.h`](ViewOwl.ESP32.Client/main/config.h) — all firmware compile-time constants
- [`ViewOwl.ESP32.Client/main/lcd_init.c`](ViewOwl.ESP32.Client/main/lcd_init.c) — SPI bus init, display controller setup
- [`ViewOwl.Grabber.Engine/TemplateMetadataParser.cs`](ViewOwl.Grabber.Engine/TemplateMetadataParser.cs) — parses `data-vow-*` from HTML body element

## Template system

Templates are self-describing HTML files. `data-vow-*` attributes on `<body>` define class, name, category, frame count, fps, refresh interval. Metadata is **not stored in DB** — parsed from `HtmlContent` on every read.

Three classes:
- **A** — any HTML/CSS, server-rendered by Chromium, single frame, refreshed periodically
- **B** — canvas-only, server grab OR live browser push (reads canvas pixels, POSTs BGR565 to device)
- **C** — canvas multi-frame animation, each frame grabbed at `?vow_frame=N`, stored in ESP32 flash, plays offline

Class C constraint: `Math.random()` forbidden — same frame index must always produce same pixels (CRC dedup breaks otherwise; also causes ARM64 Chrome timeout during batch capture via `getImageData()`).

## Frame format

Raw BGR565, 16 bits/pixel, little-endian. 480×320 = 307,200 bytes. 320×240 = 153,600 bytes. Matches native SPI LCD format — no conversion on device. Compressed variants (palette+RLE, palette+LZ4) flagged by first byte (0x01, 0x03).

## UDP protocol

15-byte header: Magic (0xABADBABE) + PacketType + SessionId + Seq + PayloadLength + Flags. 1400-byte packets. Custom ACK per chunk. NOT_MODIFIED response when device CRC matches manifest batch CRC — skips retransmission.
